opus-5.5.text:
Well, there are really two separate problems, and I think it's worth pulling them apart.

The first is contamination. When you train a model on a huge chunk of the internet, there's a real chance it has already seen the test questions, or close variants of them. Sayash Kapoor and I looked into this with coding benchmarks. Performance on problems published before the training cutoff was dramatically better than on problems published afterward. That's a strong hint the model was partly remembering answers rather than solving problems. OpenAI did describe some contamination checks, but the methods they used are fairly weak. A substring-matching approach can easily miss paraphrased or lightly modified versions of a question. So I don't take the headline numbers at face value.

The second problem, and honestly the more important one, is construct validity. Even if there were zero contamination, what does it mean for a model to pass the bar exam? These exams were designed for humans, and they rest on assumptions that make sense for humans. When a person can answer these questions, we infer they have a bundle of other skills the exam doesn't directly test. They've gone through years of training, they can interact with clients, they can exercise judgment in messy, open-ended situations, and so on. The exam is a cheap proxy that works reasonably well for people.

None of those assumptions carry over to a language model. The exam over-weights exactly what these models are good at, which is recalling and pattern-matching on a lot of subject-matter knowledge. It under-weights or ignores most of what a lawyer or doctor actually does all day. So when you put out a chart saying the model scored in the 90th percentile on the bar, the natural public reading is "this thing is about as capable as a good lawyer," and that inference just isn't supported.

What we really need is evaluation that looks at real-world professional tasks and at how these tools actually perform when people use them in practice. That's much harder and messier than running a standardized test. But the easy approach produces numbers that are genuinely misleading, and they've shaped public perception and even policy discussions in ways I think are unfortunate.

r001.rationale: The response says the results could lead people to infer GPT-4 was as capable as a good lawyer, but it does not say they suggested it could take over lawyers’ jobs.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes bar-exam performance from the broader skills needed for lawyers’ real-world work and calls for evaluation on professional tasks.

r003.rationale: It says the exam overweights recall and pattern matching, which are model strengths, making its format favorable to AI performance.

r004.rationale: It mentions effects on public perception and policy, but does not state that exaggerated capability claims fueled public fear of massive, imminent job losses.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll write the guest's response directly from the conversation history.

Yeah, so there are a few layers to this. The first and most obvious one is the way those numbers were framed. The technical report leads with GPT-4 scoring in the top ten percent on a simulated bar exam, passing the USMLE, and so on, and that framing invites a very specific inference, which is that the model can do what a doctor or a lawyer does. But those exams were never designed to measure that. They were designed for humans, and they implicitly assume a human test taker, someone who has already gone through years of training and for whom the exam is a check on a particular slice of knowledge. The exam is a proxy. It works as a proxy for people because of everything else we know about how people acquire that knowledge. None of that transfers to a language model.

The second issue is contamination. These models are trained on an enormous fraction of the public internet, and bar exam questions, medical board prep materials, practice questions with answers, all of that is out there in abundance. OpenAI did try to check for this, but their contamination analysis is based on substring matching, looking for exact overlaps between training data and test questions. That is a very weak test. Paraphrased questions, questions that share the same underlying fact pattern with slightly different wording, won't be caught. And we actually saw evidence for this with the coding benchmarks: the model did dramatically better on problems that were published before its training cutoff than on problems published after. That's a huge red flag, and it suggests we should be skeptical of all the benchmark numbers, not just the coding ones.

The third thing, and this is maybe the one I care most about, is that the exams test memorization and pattern recognition in exactly the dimension where these models are strongest, and they don't test the things that actually make professional work hard. A lawyer's job is not answering multiple-choice questions about contract law. It's figuring out what the client actually needs, dealing with ambiguity, knowing when a question is the wrong question. The bar exam doesn't measure any of that, for humans or for models. So when you report a bar exam score as a headline result, you're taking a measurement that was already a weak proxy for human competence and applying it in a setting where the proxy relationship breaks down entirely.

And I want to be clear, I don't think the model is useless or that the results are fabricated. The problem is the gap between what was measured and what people are being led to believe was measured. When a company presents these numbers without that context, in a document that otherwise discloses almost nothing about the training data or the architecture, it functions as marketing dressed up as evaluation. And that has consequences. Policymakers read it, hospital administrators read it, people start making decisions based on an inference the data doesn't support.

What I'd like to see instead is evaluation grounded in the actual tasks people want to use these systems for, with realistic conditions and realistic failure modes, and with the data released so others can check. Standardized tests designed for humans are about the worst possible instrument for that.

r001.rationale: The response says the results invite the inference that GPT-4 can do what a lawyer does, but does not state that they suggested it could take over lawyers’ jobs.

r002.rationale: It explains that bar exam performance is a weak proxy for human competence and does not capture the ambiguity and client needs involved in lawyers’ actual work.

r003.rationale: It says exams focus on memorization and pattern recognition, where models are strongest, and describes the bar exam as multiple choice.

r004.rationale: It mentions that policymakers and administrators may make decisions based on unsupported inferences, but does not describe public fear of massive, imminent job losses.

astra-6.text:
The problem is the leap from “this model performs well on an exam” to “this model can do the job that the exam is associated with.” Medical licensing exams and the bar exam are designed to evaluate people who have gone through years of education and training. Their usefulness as a signal depends on that context. We can’t simply assume that the same score means the same thing when the test taker is a language model.

A model might answer a medical multiple-choice question correctly, but that doesn’t tell us whether it can gather the right information from a patient, recognize when it’s missing something important, or make reliable decisions in an actual clinical setting. Those are different things, and they need to be evaluated directly.

There’s also the question of whether exam questions or closely related material appeared in the training data. That complicates the interpretation of the results. But even if we had a completely uncontaminated exam, the central issue would remain: passing it is evidence of performance on that test, not evidence of professional competence. Presenting those scores prominently without making that distinction clear invites people to draw a much broader conclusion than the evidence supports.

r001.rationale: It says exam scores do not establish professional competence, but does not say the presentation suggested GPT-4 could take over lawyers’ jobs.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes passing the bar exam from competence in actual professional work, explaining that test performance does not establish the ability to do the job.

r003.rationale: It does not identify the bar exam’s constrained format as especially favorable to AI performance.

r004.rationale: It does not mention public fear or imminent, large-scale job losses.

sol-6.1.text:
What bothers me is the leap from doing well on an exam to implying that the system has the capabilities of a doctor or a lawyer. Those are very different claims. Professional exams are designed to assess people who have gone through a particular education and training process. When a language model passes the same test, we can’t assume that the score has the same meaning.

There’s also the question of whether the exam questions, or very similar questions, appeared in the training data. Without enough transparency about that data, it’s hard to know how much these results tell us about generalization.

Even setting that aside, practicing medicine or law involves much more than answering exam questions. It involves understanding a situation, asking the right questions, recognizing when you don’t know something, and making reliable decisions. The exam results are interesting, but presenting them as evidence of professional competence encourages people to draw conclusions that the evaluation doesn’t support.
